sections.brief: Open the stage where Stage Five ends ([scene:s11c|22 November 1963]) in one sentence, then tell how Johnson inherited Kennedy's two-track policy, in order: the 'icebox' approach; the Harman–Gazit–Ron request to Bundy and Komer (300 Shermans, 200 M48A3s and 100 M60s, defense at about 40% of the budget and 11% of GNP) and Bundy's reply on missiles, the 'existing nuclear potential' and the Jordan waters; the early-1964 decision to refuse a direct tank sale but help through Europe; Eshkol's 1–2 June 1964 visit (the first official visit by an Israeli prime minister, the 'could not provide tanks directly' and 'we back Israel fully on the Jordan water' exchanges, the joint statement and desalting); and the Dimona-reassurance-to-Nasser dispute from March to 2 June 1964 and Komer's four concessions. Close with the parallel Egyptian track (Nasser's July 1964 no-nuclear pledge, McCloy's failed missile mission, the P.L. 480 slide to June 1966) so the reader sees Washington balancing both capitals. Present the dispute on whether the visit changed arms policy from both sides. Figure: timeline November 1963–July 1964.

The Arab side of 1964 in its own terms: Nasser's 23 December 1963 invitation; the Cairo summit of 13–17 January 1964 (the communiqué's wording on the diversion, 'organizing the Palestinian people', self-determination, the truce in media campaigns; the Unified Arab Command); Shuqairi's mandate; the Jerusalem congress of 28 May–2 June 1964 (about 400 appointed delegates under Hussein's sponsorship, the PLO, the Charter and Basic Law); the Alexandria summit of September 1964 over Syrian and Saudi objections; Casablanca 1965; the PLA and the CIA's December 1966 picture; and Hussein's break with the PLO in July 1966. Quote the Charter's Articles 2, 7, 17, 18 and 24 exactly and present the Article 24 dispute (critics' reading vs Rabbani's) without adjudicating. Present the 'who created the PLO' question from both the League/Nasser and the Palestinian-congress angles. Name the Charter's denial of Israel's legitimacy plainly, and do not generalize about Palestinians or Arabs. Figure: timeline December 1963–July 1966.

The Jews of the Arab world between Suez and June 1967, picking up where [scene:rd6_exodus|the exodus of 1948–56] stops (one sentence; do not retell): Egypt after Suez (the 1948 and post-1948 population estimates; about 1,000 arrests; the 13,000 British and French expellees and 500 others; the 15 November 1956 order and the 'voluntary' renunciation forms; 8,500 by sea by February 1957; about 25,000 gone in 1956 and some 15,000 left in 1957; sequestrations), then Morocco's Operation Yachin from 28 November 1961 (Hassan II–Ben-Gurion understanding; more than 97,000 by 1964; the per-head payments and the $50 million from HIAS). Present the 'expelled vs emigrated' dispute (Beinin and Julius vs Bizawe) fairly; name antisemitic measures plainly where documented and do not generalize about Arabs or Muslims. Label Fathom and the CIE timeline as advocacy/educational sources. State plainly that Iraq, Syria, Libya and Yemen in 1956–67 were not researched. Figure: timeline November 1956–1964.

The water war, 1964–66, picking up sy_s02's DMZ thread where Stage Two leaves the Johnston Plan (one linking sentence): the Johnston technical plan of 1955 and why the League did not ratify it; the Carrier entering operation in 1964 (10 June 1964 per the Center for Israel Education, a secondary date; say so) (212 metres of lift, 320 million cubic metres a year, 'within the Johnston allocations' per Wolf); the Arab options weighed in January 1964 and the September 1964 choice of diversion; the Hasbani–Litani and Banias–Yarmuk scheme (Mukheiba, up to 125 million cubic metres a year), Lebanon's July 1965 halt; the Israeli strikes of March, May and August 1965 and the 1966 abandonment; Washington's position (backing Israel on the water while urging no preemption). Tell from sy_s02 only its 1964–67 water-war entity and Dayan's later '80 percent' remark as his own 1976 account, contested. Present the disputes on how the works were hit (tank fire vs bombing) and on the first sabotage attempt (31 December 1964 vs 1–2 January 1965; PLO vs Fatah), linking cw6_fatah. Embed map syria_line and discuss its 'DMZ & water war' stage. Figure: process flow of the two water schemes.

Palestinian citizens of Israel as political actors under military government, 1959–65: the Popular Front of 1959 and al-Ard's emergence (El-Asmar as a founder), the closed newspapers and refused registration, the 1964 Jiryis judgment and the Defense Minister's ban, the 29 September 1965 rejection of the Socialists' List and the Yeredor appeal (Agranat and Sussman's 'defensive democracy' majority; Cohn's dissent on section 23, quoted). Add the 1963 Knesset vote that failed by one, with Muadi and Ubaid. Present the dispute (defence of the state vs suppression of organizing) with each side's strongest case, and label Konrad's 2015 essay as advocacy-journalism interpretation. Link back to [scene:rd6_military_government|military government] for the regime itself; do not retell it. Figure: comparison of the majority and the dissent in Yeredor.

How Bonn's secret arms became recognition, October 1964–August 1965, with one sentence linking back to the 1952 reparations told in [scene:rd6_financing|financing the new state] and the 1957 Strauss–Peres origins (Stage Four): Rusk's October 1964 figures (150 M48A1s 'as is', about 250 Centurions; the 82-tank option; the $24 million kits on MAP credit; conversion in Italy 'in the interests of secrecy'; the 15 November 1964 cancellation clause); the October 1964 leak; Nasser's invitation to Ulbricht and Bonn's halt; Ulbricht in Egypt from 24 February 1965; Erhard's 7 March decision taken over his cabinet's head and Birrenbach learning it in Tel Aviv; the 140 million DM settlement; 12 May 1965 and Pauls's credentials on 19 August. Explain the Hallstein Doctrine as the mechanism. Present both disputes (thirteen ambassadors withdrawn vs ten states breaking relations; Ulbricht leaving 1 or 2 March). Close with JTA's March 1965 report that 1965–66 was the agreement's last year (300 million marks of goods that year; 2.4 billion received in goods), and say that the reported total does not reconcile with the 3 billion DM headline. Figure: money chain for the German tank deal (German stocks → Italy/US kits → Israel → who gained → the cost when it leaked).

Fatah's armed campaign from its first operation to spring 1967. Give the first operation in all three documented versions side by side (IPS: dawn 1 January 1965, Ahmad Musa killed; Morris: night of 2 January, charge defused, leader shot after a Jordanian patrol intercepted the squad; Wolf: 31 December 1964, 'the PLO's first action') without choosing. Then the record: Syrian sponsorship (base, training, propaganda); the 61 incidents Israel attributed to Fatah by December 1966; Kuwaiti and Saudi private money; raids from Jordanian and Lebanese territory without those governments' approval; Israeli reprisals on the West Bank from May 1965; U Thant's May 1967 judgment. From ilb_s04 tell only the 1965–May 1967 part (Khashan's 'quiet until around 1965', the Lebanese army's response and the sectarian split) and link the war and the 1968 PLO takeover forward to [scene:s12|the June war]. Examine the term 'terrorism' as used in the sources (CIA, U Thant) rather than assuming it. Figure: timeline January 1965–April 1967.

From the German route to the first direct US tank sale, February–July 1965: the Jordan problem (Hussein's warning of Soviet aircraft; the February 1965 decision to sell him tanks); Eshkol's reaction; the Harriman–Komer mission and the conditions Israel refused (inspections, water pledge, UN referral); the memorandum transmitted by Barbour on 10 March 1965, quoted clause by clause (security commitment; 'will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Arab-Israel area'; 'at least the same number and quality of tanks that it sells to Jordan'; the German M48s; aircraft 'if not from Western sources, then from the United States'; secrecy), and the FRUS editors' gloss (up to 24 aircraft, 11 March). Then Komer's 29 July 1965 close: 110 M48A2Cs plus 100 M48A1s, about $42 million, kits for the 40 German tanks, and Rusk's resistance to planes. Present the wording dispute over the nuclear pledge across 1965–66. Embed aid_arms:Overview:2 and discuss its 1962 step (first military aid, as loans) against what 1965 changed. Figure: comparison of what Israel asked for (doc. 7) and what it got (March and July 1965).

NUMEC's start, 1957–1967, now from the primary record (National Security Archive briefing book 565), with the 1968 CIA–Helms request, the Eitan visit and the 1978 GAO study linked forward. Tell in order: NUMEC's founding in 1957 and HEU processing at Apollo; the early-1965 AEC shortage; Shapiro's 10 August 1965 admission of earlier payments 'up to $1 million'; the November 1965 inventory; Seaborg's 14 February 1966 'an inquiry by the FBI is not now warranted'; the April 1966 figure (178 kg U-235, 93.8 kg unexplained); the FBI's June 1966 FARA interview and ISORAD; GAO's June 1967 260 kg. Keep each figure with its unit, date and source and present the quantity dispute (including the scene's '206 pounds' and 269 kg). Keep the scene's discipline and the editors': evidence 'strong but not incontrovertible', the AEC found no evidence of theft, no one was charged. Set it briefly beside the Dimona visits of 1964–66 (Eshkol's 'invited guests'; the 1966 team's missing 80–100 tons of Argentine concentrate). Figure: timeline 1957–June 1967 of the inventory findings.

Syria's radical turn, 1963–66: the 1963 Ba'th takeover and Amin al-Hafiz, the rise of Jadid and Assad, the coup of 23 February 1966 ('the bloodiest' since 1949 per GlobalSecurity, labelled as that source), Atassi, Zuayyin and Assad at defense from 1 March, Hatum's failed countercoup of 8 September, and the Egypt–Syria five-year defense pact of November 1966. Explain the mechanism that tied Syria to Fatah (base, training, propaganda, per the CIA) and the Soviet backing only as far as the sources date it. Present the dispute on who drove the Syrian front (Israeli threats per the Library of Congress and Laurens vs Syrian sponsorship of raids per the CIA). Keep the 7 April 1967 air battle for cw6_april_1967. Embed map syria_line and discuss its 1949–67 stages.

The two tracks as they stood in 1966, built on s11d but corrected by the research. Narrative: the 12 February 1966 White House meeting (48 aircraft, the A-4E, the A-6 refused, Johnson's 'twelve Congressmen'), McNamara's offer to Eban (24 plus 24, about $26 million, Hawk terms) and his conditions (Europe first; 'not to be the first power in the Middle East to manufacture nuclear weapons'; periodic Dimona inspection; no nuclear carriers; secrecy), Komer's report of the deal (48 A-4Es, about $50 million; 36 F-104s for Jordan, cash, from 1968; 'unless others do'), and the first four Skyhawks reaching Haifa on 29 December 1967. Then the inspection track: the 1966 visit (dates disputed: 31 March–1 April vs 31 March–4 April), its findings, the 11 June 1966 demand for six-monthly visits and the plutonium arithmetic, Rusk's warning, the concealed reprocessing plant and the nine AEC teams of 1961–69 per Burr and Cohen. Engage the scene's claim-and-record box: the arms relationship predates 1967, but correct three scene details plainly: the Hawk was an air-defence missile, the M48s came in 1965 via Germany and then by direct sale, and the visit count and 'staged control rooms' are not in the fetched sources; flag the FRUS summary's '48 F-4s' as an error. Present the dispute on whether the visits were a real check, and the scene's own discipline that no document states an explicit trade. Figure: comparison of the 1965 and 1966 nuclear wordings; timeline of the six arms decisions 1964–66.

Samu, 11–25 November 1966, from the UN record first: the mine that killed three Israeli soldiers (Fatah per the IDF archives; the PLF per the CIA; 11 or 12 November) and the raid of 13 November (Operation Magressa) as UNTSO's S/7593 reconstructs it hour by hour, saying which details rest on Jordanian witnesses; the damage (125 houses, clinic, six-classroom school; Kh. Jimba; the police post) and the casualty figures with UNTSO's internal discrepancy and the CIA's 'about 50'. Then Washington: Rostow's 'out of all proportion' and 'wrong target', Sisco's 'dismayed', the CIA's warning for Hussein's throne, West Bank riots, Resolution 228 (14–0–1, New Zealand abstaining, the US in favour) quoted, Johnson's letter to Hussein and his warning to Israel of suspended shipments, and the Jordan aid request ($200 million) and December package. Give the Israeli rationale and the American and Jordanian objections each in their strongest form. Figure: timeline 11–25 November 1966 (and, if room, a comparison of the casualty counts).

The end of military government only (the regime and Kafr Qasim are told in Volume II and Stage Three; link [scene:rd6_military_government|the regime] in one sentence and do not retell): Shamgar's 1963 manual; Eshkol's 21 October 1963 cancellation of personal permits and Tzur's 3 November 1963 directive (zones cut from 17 to nine, eleven villages kept closed); the 18 November 1965 village review; the 12 January 1966 Knesset statement; Harel's 27 February 1966 directives (Shin Bet reinforced, police stations, a 'mixed communities' unit and a demolition unit); JTA's 150,000; notice on 8 November and abolition on 1 December 1966. Then what remained: Regulations 109–112 and 125, Toledano's 'psychological' change, and the IPS dating of full abolition to late 1968. From mg_s01 tell only its closing fact (abolished 1966) and link the rest back. Present the dispute on whether 1 December 1966 ended military rule. Figure: process flow showing which body took each power in 1966.

Israel at home, 1965–67, so the reader knows the country that entered the May crisis: Ben-Gurion's break and Rafi (Lavon, the Alignment, Eshkol), the 2 November 1965 election (turnout, seats per list, the blocs' losses, Rafi's disappointing 10; the vote-count discrepancy for Rafi), Eshkol's 75-member coalition; then the recession from the Bank of Israel's own 1966 report (GNP +0.6% vs +8.2%; investment −18.4%; construction; unemployment 3.6% → 7.4% → 10.3% in the last quarter; job seekers 5,463 → 19,376; net immigration's share of growth 49% → 12%; emigration), the Bank's explanation and the policy reversal it judged too late. Close by linking forward to the 1 June unity government in cw6_tiran_june4. Figure: comparison table 1965 vs 1966 indicators.

Egypt's posture by spring 1967: the Yemen intervention from September 1962 (the commando company, Nasser's '70,000', Saudi supply of the royalists, the 1965 Jeddah attempt), its cost (Riedel's 25,000 casualties vs Foreign Policy's at least 10,000 dead, as different measures), forces still in Yemen in May 1967 (number unverified; say so), and Rogan and Aclimandos's thesis that the campaign 'fatally impaired' Egypt in June 1967 without being the sole cause. Add the CIA's 23 May and end-May judgments (Israel could take Sinai in 'several days'; Arab unity 'fiction') as Washington's reading of the balance. Link the Khartoum withdrawal forward.

The border with Syria in spring 1967: the 7 April 1967 land and air engagement and the six Syrian aircraft shot down (Fanack; Laurens's reading that it exposed Nasser's inaction); Rabin's statement that Damascus's 'authorities are behind the terrorists' and Eshkol's warning about 'the last 14 incidents', both as Tal gives them; the Library of Congress summary of Israeli threats; and the November 1966 Egypt–Syria pact as the hinge that made a Syrian front Cairo's problem. Present both readings of who was escalating (Israeli pressure vs Syrian-sponsored raids) with their sources. Short section; end on 12 May, linking to cw6_may_crisis.

13–21 May 1967 from the documents: the Soviet warning of 13 May (about 11 brigades per Elbahtimy; two brigades per the Library of Congress) through three channels; Fawzi on the Syrian border on 14 May (state that the archive catalogue does not record his conclusions); the 17 May cabinet's 'mainly for show' assumption; Fawzi's 16 May letter to Rikhye (quoted) and U Thant's same-day reply; Riad's 18 May request and the Advisory Committee; UNEF's 3,378 men from seven countries and Israel's refusal to host it; U Thant's consent argument and his ruling on Hammarskjöld's 1957 note; his 19 May report (UNTSO found no concentrations; Israeli statements 'particularly inflammatory'; 'more menacing' than since 1956); Kosygin and Eshkol's letters. Present the three positions on Soviet motive (Ginor and Remez; Elbahtimy; Tal) and the two on Nasser's aims, and the date discrepancies for the UNEF request, without adjudicating beyond the documents. Figure: timeline 13–21 May 1967.

The stage's last section, 22 May–4 June 1967, ending on 4 June. Nasser's 22 May speech and 26 May statement quoted exactly; U Thant in Cairo and Israel's casus belli; the Israeli cabinet's 23, 26 and 27 May deadlock; Rabin's 'to be or not to be' and Yariv's warning beside Tal's note that Rabin saw no intent on 22 May; Johnson and Eban on 26 May (no imminent attack; 'not be alone unless it decides to go it alone'; constitutional processes); Kosygin and Badran in Moscow; the 30 May Egypt–Jordan pact; Dayan and Begin on 1 June; Amit and McNamara (the record vs Amit's 1992 recollection); Johnson's 3 June letter; the 4 June decision in both published wordings and Lozowick's reading of the transcripts (no formal dissent; Barzilai and Bentov); state that the vote count is unsettled ('a majority of 18' per the IDF archive; no tally in the transcripts' reading). Present the existential-threat, green-light and Tiran-closure disputes with each side's documents, and say what the record does not settle. End by linking forward to [scene:s12|the Six-Day War] and [scene:iaa_s04|who fired first]; tell nothing of 5 June. Figure: timeline 22 May–4 June 1967.
